items.title: ‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?
items.summary:
Gladestry primary school is predicted to have only 19 pupils within two years, while its county council is forced to make cuts year after year. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for

The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling.

From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football.

items.title: These maps show how expensive state schools can be for low-income students
items.summary:
To avoid spending their young adult lives in debt, students have long been counseled to stay in-state for college. After all, it’s the mission of public universities, funded by tax dollars, to provide an affordable, high-quality education to state residents. 

Yet, in 34 states, it costs students from low-income families at least a third of their household income — upwards of $10,000 a year — to attend the state flagship university. That includes not just tuition, but also room and board and books, after accounting for all grants and scholarships — what’s known as “net price.” 

Take Alabama, which had one of the highest price tags for public colleges in the country in 2024, the most recent data available. A student coming from a family in that state that earns less than $30,000 a year was expected to pay more than $19,000 annually on average for tuition and other costs at the University of Alabama, the flagship. The same went for Pennsylvania State University.

And it’s not just flagship universities. At more than half of four-year public colleges across the country, including regional public institutions as well as large research universities, in-state students from families making less than $30,000 faced this same, near-impossible financial juggling act: On average, they had to pay more than a third of their family income to attend. 

Net price at public colleges has declined over the past few years, when adjusted to overall inflation, yet wages have not kept up as the costs of housing, food and health care keep rising, and low-income families continue to struggle to…
items.t: These maps show how expensive state schools can be for low-income students

Students who completed a Colorado college program in 2017-18 earned about 55% more than state residents with only a high school diploma, according to a new study. That gap, called a wage premium, was the second lowest in the country.

Colorado degree or certificate holders earned about $61,000 a year on average in the four years after graduating, according to the data from The HEA Group, which studies the value of higher education. High school diploma holders earned about $39,000 a year in the four years after graduating. While that’s a difference of more than $20,000, it still falls short of the national average of closer to $26,000 and a 76% wage premium.

Michael Itzkowitz, The HEA Group president, said Colorado’s high school diploma holders have higher pay than the national average. Colorado also has a higher percentage of students who completed college programs with low earnings. And while the state’s bachelor’s and certificate earners make at least the national average, Colorado associate degree holders earn less.

Colorado advocates and college leaders say the data has prompted discussions about whether the state should have more oversight and if students have the information they need to select college programs.

items.title: Three studies in a row show teeny-tiny or zero academic gains from school cellphone bans
items.summary:
Since 2023, cellphone use during the school day has been banned or restricted in at least 40 states and the District of Columbia, in the hope that reducing digital distractions would help students focus on their lessons.

So how’s it working?

Last week researchers at Harvard University released the third major study of cellphone limits in U.S. schools and, like the two before it, it found remarkably little academic benefit. Media reports trumpeted the study’s findings of gains in student achievement as evidence of real progress . But read the fine print: Students’ combined math and reading scores, as measured by MAP tests, rose by only an extra 0.0087 of a standard deviation.

Readers, I try to avoid talking about abstract statistical units, but in this case, they’re important because they show just how teeny-tiny the academic gains were. The estimated improvement is less than one-hundredth of a standard deviation, a very small shift in student performance. In graduate school, I was taught that even an improvement of one-tenth of a standard deviation — more than 10 times the size of this effect — is quite small.

But the Harvard researchers translated that 0.0087 improvement into one to two weeks of additional learning a year. They characterized the gains as “modest” and said they could add up over time and help students recover half of the learning losses that accumulated between 2013 and 2020, before student performance took a steeper nosedive during the pandemic.

The tiny gain was found after comparing student achievement in schools where students had to put their…
items.t: Three studies in a row show teeny-tiny or zero academic gains from school cellphone bans

items.title: OPINION: It’s time to put curiosity, creativity and critical thinking first in the early learning years
items.summary:
Early education is often judged by how quickly children master the 3 Rs: reading, writing and arithmetic. Those skills are essential, but not sufficient.

Children also need the 3 Cs: curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

We often treat the 3 Cs as “nice-to-haves” after children master reading, writing and arithmetic. But that gets the sequence backward.

Curiosity draws a child toward a book. Creativity links ideas in new ways as the child reads. Critical thinking helps the child assess whether those ideas fit together.

The 3 Cs are not a reward for finishing the academic work. Instead, they drive learning and make it stick.

Few educators would argue that the 3 Cs are unimportant. The problem is that we have organized early education around the 3 Rs . Further, our approach to these basic skills often reflects a predominantly academic style of teaching in the early years, with a proliferation of scripted curricula, worksheets, drills and questions with a single expected answer. I propose weaving the 3 Cs into early learning at school and at home through rich, back-and-forth conversations, open-ended questions and guided play.

Related: Young children have unique needs and providing the right care can be a challenge. Our free early childhood education newsletter tracks the issues.

items.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
items.summary:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. On a late spring day in 1995, Mayor Richard M. Daley called his chief budget and finance director, Paul Vallas, into his City Hall office.

Republican lawmakers, responding to a prolonged financial and governance crisis in Chicago Public Schools, were going to hand control of the district to the mayor. Daley told the 42-year-old Vallas, a hard-charging number-cruncher lacking management experience in public education, that he wanted him to be the district’s first CEO.

“He didn’t really ask me,” Vallas said. “I was eager to do it.”

Thus began three decades of mayoral governance that would take Chicago Public Schools from being labeled as the worst in the nation to a national leader of education reform to a district struggling with enrollment declines. It gave Chicago’s mayor authority to appoint everyone on the Chicago Board of Education, and effectively final say over major decisions that affected schools.

The board voted 4-2 to appoint Caron Blanke to represent central-east Denver’s District 3. Board Vice President Monica Hunter and members Amy Klein Molk, Kimberlee Sia, and John Youngquist voted yes. President Xóchitl Gaytán and member Marlene De La Rosa voted no.

A conservative group that led a failed bid to counteract Amendment 87 filed a lawsuit on Thursday to overturn the measure, alleging the amendment to overhaul Colorado’s tax code violated the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights, or TABOR, and misled voters about its impact.

The lawsuit, filed in Denver District Court by Advance Colorado on behalf of state Republican Sens. Barbara Kirkmeyer and Byron Pelton alleges new revenue raised by the measure won’t go toward education and that the state gave voters incorrect information about how much money some taxpayers would save.

Gov. Jared Polis and the director of Colorado’s Department of Revenue are listed as defendants. A Polis administration spokesperson declined to comment on the pending litigation.

Less than a year ago, Philadelphia school officials said eliminating hundreds of substitute teacher positions would save millions.

Now they’re asking for millions more to cover substitute staffing costs.

Last March, Superintendent Tony Watlington and Chief Financial Officer Mike Herbstman said cutting more than 200 building substitute positions would save the district $13 million, and help the district close a $300 million budget hole.

But at Thursday’s school board meeting, the district asked the board to approve a contract amendment that would award a substitute staffing company, ESS Northeast LLC, an additional $11 million “to maintain essential substitute staffing services in the absence of employees across all District schools.”

Board members approved the amended contract unanimously without discussion Thursday evening.

Nearly two-thirds of New York City public schools lost enrollment over the past year, according to newly released school level numbers.

The school-by-school data offers the most granular look yet at how kindergarten to 12th grade enrollment in the nation’s largest school system dropped by 23,000 this year — the largest year-over-year drop since the COVID-19 pandemic. Nearly 1,100 of the city’s roughly 1,600 schools have fewer students than last year, a Chalkbeat analysis found. (Scroll to the bottom of the story to look up how each school’s enrollment changed over the past year.)

As Denver Mayor Mike Johnston pitches universal childcare as a way to keep the city affordable, the city’s 20-year-old preschool tuition assistance program is expanding its mission to focus on children from birth to age 5.

Leaders of the Denver Preschool Program announced the creation of First Step Collective, a new citywide umbrella organization, during a press event Thursday morning at the Blossom House community building in the Westwood neighborhood.

The new organization will include the Denver Preschool Program as well as other early childhood groups, programs, and services. It will be fully operational by August 2028, said Elsa Holguín, president and CEO of the Denver Preschool Program.

The preschool program’s expansion comes as infant and toddler care remains a major pain point for working parents and state and local governments experiment with increasingly ambitious early childhood efforts. The Pennsylvania State Board of Education rejected the Department of Education’s proposal to change how it scores students on standardized tests Thursday.

Department of Education Deputy Secretary Amy Lena said the decision means it will take more time for districts to get official results for the roughly 900,000 students statewide who took the Pennsylvania System of School Assessment, or PSSA, and high school Keystone tests in the spring.

“We will just have to go back, we’ll have to make sure that we run them under the old (scoring system),” Lena said. “That will take a little bit of time.”

State officials shared the controversial proposal to change the “cut scores” two weeks ago. They said changing the thresholds would make the scoring system more accurate and result in more students being deemed “advanced.” But several board members said they were concerned that communication about the plan had been rushed, with insufficient time for public feedback.
